title: How Nitrous Oxide Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain nitrous oxide ("laughing gas," "hippie crack"), telling its history out of order: Horace Wells' failed 1845 Harvard demonstration and later decline, Joseph Priestley's gas research and pneumatic trough, Humphrey Davy's 1799 Boxing Day experiments and his book on nitrous oxide, and its later use as an anesthetic. They cover how it works in the body (analgesic, dissociative anesthetic, anxiolytic), its use in cars and whipped cream, recreational use and its dangers (oxygen displacement, deaths from bags or canisters), a study on brain effects, the 2016 UK legalization debate, and its use in childbirth. The episode ends with a listener mail segment.

segments.title: Opening banter and episode setup
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode on nitrous oxide and say they will tell its history out of order.

segments.title: Horace Wells and the Humbug affair
segments.summary: Dentist Horace Wells sees a demonstration by Gardner Quincy Colton, uses nitrous oxide for painless tooth extraction, then fails at a Harvard demonstration, the Humbug affair. His later decline and death in prison are described.

segments.title: Joseph Priestley and the pneumatic trough
segments.summary: Joseph Priestley, an Enlightenment thinker, studies gases and uses a pneumatic trough, a device Stephen Hales first created, to isolate gases.

segments.title: Humphrey Davy's Boxing Day experiments
segments.summary: Humphrey Davy inhales large amounts of nitrous oxide in December 1799 and describes the effects. Robert Southey is brought in, and Davy invites others to experiment, finding language inadequate to describe the experience.

segments.title: Davy's treatise and nitrous oxide as anesthetic
segments.summary: Davy's 1800 treatise notes nitrous oxide may relieve pain in surgery. Decades later Wells and the medical field adopt it, and it becomes the top inhaled anesthetic.

segments.title: How nitrous oxide works in the body
segments.summary: Nitrous oxide acts as an analgesic, a dissociative anesthetic, and an anxiolytic. It affects opioid receptors, NMDA receptors, and the spinal column. It is metabolized very little and exhaled unchanged, so there is no hangover.

segments.title: Whipped cream and cars
segments.summary: Nitrous oxide is used as a propellant in whipped cream canisters and dispenses fresh whip because it displaces oxygen. Nitrous oxide injected into car engines adds oxygen to boost power, as seen in Fast and Furious.

segments.title: Recreational use and the 1970s concert scene
segments.summary: Recreational nitrous use took off in the 1970s at concerts and festivals. Its short-lived high is explained by fast clearance from the body. Early Hollywood films about laughing gas are mentioned.

segments.title: Brain effects and dangers
segments.summary: A clinical neurophysiology study found brain wave changes lasting about three minutes after use. Rat studies suggest brain cell damage from prolonged or high-concentration exposure. Oxygen displacement causes hypoxia, and the drug can kill through suffocation or injury.

segments.title: UK legalization debate and deaths
segments.summary: Nitrous oxide was legal in the UK until 2016, when it was classified as a drug. Festival litter and deaths from canisters and bags are discussed, with a charity saying the risk is relatively low when used from balloons.

segments.title: L. Ron Hubbard and Scientology's view
segments.summary: L. Ron Hubbard reportedly had a near-death experience under nitrous oxide at the dentist, which led him to write against the drug in Dianetics and his unpublished manuscript.

segments.title: Nitrous oxide in childbirth
segments.summary: Women in Canada, Finland, Australia, and the UK use nitrous oxide for labor pain. Hospitals in the US rarely offer it. It is self-administered, cheap, and thought to pose no harm to the baby.

segments.title: Closing and sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts close the episode with a pointer to the next part of listener mail and a web search suggestion.
